articles.title_orig: CVS to Split Off Drugstore Business, Ending Its Bigger-Is-Better Era
articles.title_zh: CVS to Split Off Drugstore Business, Ending Its Bigger-Is-Better Era
articles.content_orig:
CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate breakups in history, the company announced Wednesday.
The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs.
The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release . Shares of CVS fell roughly 11% on Wednesday.
It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS' aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs.
But Joyner told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday that the decision to split is "out of a position of strength," pointing to recovery in Aetna's Medicare business and solid performance in the retail pharmacy.
"So it's all about the strength of the business that affords us the opportunity to make what we think are the right strategic decisions for the future of this company," he later added.
CVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion.
The two new companies would both be publicly traded.
The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said.
Existing CVS shareholders will own shares in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans.
The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion.
CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period.
Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company's health care benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year.
On Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home-visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business.
CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits.
It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units.
But Joyner told CNBC that the company was "in a turnaround" at that time without the flexibility, cash position or business performance to execute a split.
In an interview, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split shows "the stability of the pharmacy," which has won market share from competitors and is seeing gross margins stabilize thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year that the company bills as more transparent.
"This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome," he told CNBC on Wednesday.
One potential concern for investors is whether the retail pharmacy will lose its competitive advantage of being directly linked with a PBM, which negotiates drug prices and manages prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers.
But Joyner told analysts Wednesday that the synergy between the two businesses "are going to be preserved in commercial agreements between the two organizations," adding that "we don't need the integration of an operating structure."
Cherny said the rationale for the split could also extend to the state legislative scrutiny over the company's level of vertical integration.
The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states. Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban co-ownership of PBMs and pharmacies. Those have been challenged in court by CVS and other companies.
PBMs have been criticized for opaque pricing practices, their growing market power and potential conflicts of interest when they are owned by companies that also operate insurers and pharmacies.

articles.title_zh: AI data-center stocks slide, renewables rally after Democratic US midterm sweep
articles.content_orig:
Democrats scored sweeping victories in the U.S. midterm elections on Wednesday, flipping key Republican-held seats in Congress and securing historic wins in traditionally conservative states, as voters delivered a setback to President Donald Trump.
The party was projected to gain control of both chambers of Congress, with victories across several battleground states threatening to constrain Trump's legislative agenda for the remaining two years of his presidency.
Here are some of the scenes from polling stations, campaign headquarters and election-night celebrations across the United States.
Among the biggest surprises was Texas, where Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton to become the state's first Democratic U.S. senator since 1988.
Fellow Democrat Gina Hinojosa also unseated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the state's first Latina governor and ending more than three decades of Republican control of the office.
In North Carolina, former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a Republican-held Senate seat after defeating Trump-backed Michael Whatley. Cooper will succeed retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who announced his departure after clashing with Trump over his tax and spending legislation.
In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff secured reelection against Trump-backed Republican Mike Collins, while former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor's race, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a U.S. state.
Meanwhile, in Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown staged a political comeback, defeating Republican incumbent Jon Husted in a closely watched Senate race.
The elections were widely viewed as a referendum on Trump's second term, with concerns over the cost of living, inflation and the war in Iran weighing on voter sentiment.
—CNBC's Danielle DeVries contributed to this article.

articles.title_orig: Business Leaders React As a 'Blunami' Sweeps America on Election Night
articles.title_zh: Business Leaders React As a 'Blunami' Sweeps America on Election Night
articles.content_orig:
The 2026 midterm elections delivered shocking wins for Democrats on Tuesday evening, reshaping the balance of power in Washington.
Business leaders, tech executives, and investors are now assessing what the new political landscape could mean for their industries as Democratic candidates flipped key Senate and House seats.
This includes Texas, where James Talarico won his Senate race despite over $150 million in funding from Elon Musk for his Republican rival, Ken Paxton.
After the results, some of the tech and business leaders who sought closer ties with President Donald Trump ahead of his return to the White House could face new congressional scrutiny.
In California, the results of the nation's first-ever ballot measure to impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents with net worth exceeding $1 billion could have major implications for the state's elite, though as of around 7 a.m. ET, the "No" vote held a strong lead.
Here's how powerbrokers in business and tech reacted to the midterms results amid the blue wave sweeping across the country:
Reid Hoffman , the cofounder of LinkedIn and a Democratic megadonor, reacted to the party's big wins in a post on X Tuesday evening.
"Voters made clear they demand a different kind of country. Americans want an economy that can compete globally and deliver for them at home. And they made clear that they want leaders they can trust to fight for their constituents," he wrote.
"This night blew the doors off our expectations. From Texas to Ohio, Kentucky to Iowa, and South Carolina to Indiana, voters rejected the status quo. Tonight's lesson: Never discount any voter in any place," he continued.
Hoffman has been active in politics and vocal about his support for Democrats, spending tens of millions this election cycle. He also spent millions to support Kamala Harris's campaign in 2024.
Hoffman has previously said the Democratic Party had alienated Silicon Valley and was partly to blame for its shift to the right.
Elon Musk , who spent hundreds of millions to support Republicans, broke his silence late on election night with two short X posts.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said, referencing concerns that Democratic wins could mean more scrutiny on data center development.
"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," he joked in a quick follow-up post.
Musk, the world's richest person, spent more money than any other individual in the midterms, donating a whopping $446 million, mostly in Texas, the state he calls home along with his companies Tesla and SpaceX.
In addition to Talarico's Senate seat, the Texas governorship was also won by a Democrat, Gina Hinojosa. It was the first time in decades a Democrat won a statewide race in the Lone Star state.
Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, saw the election results as showing that tech companies need to do more to convince people about the benefits of AI.
"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," she said in an interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street."
"I do think this is an opportunity for us as a tech industry to realize that we need to make sure that the value proposition is clear to every local community that is going to host a data center, and I believe we can do that," she added.
Dara Khosrowshahi , the CEO of Uber, shared his thoughts on the midterms in a Wednesday morning interview with CNBC.
"I think the people of our country sent a message regarding change," he said. "I think that continuous inflation really has taken a mark on the consumer."
"I think it's up to businesses and up to our politicians and leaders in Washington to respond, and I hope that they do, because it was a very clear message that was sent out."
Khorowshahi, who is Iranian by birth, was a vocal critic of Trump during his first term, but donated $1 million to the president's inaugural fund after the 2024 election.
Keith Rabois held executive roles at PayPal, LinkedIn, and Square, before becoming managing director at Khosla Ventures. As the results came in overnight, he posted on X: "Another reason to move to Miami."
It came shortly after the Associated Press called Florida's US Senate race for the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, who held on despite a strong Democratic swing.
While two of the city's three main congressional districts elected Democrats in huge swings, the one that covers downtown Miami looks set to narrowly reelect the Republican incumbent, with 99% of the vote counted.
Rabois is married to Jacob Helberg, Trump's undersecretary of state for economic affairs, and their wedding ceremony was officiated by Sam Altman.
Last year, The Wall Street Journal reported the couple was selling their Miami Beach home for $65 million as Helberg relocated to Washington, DC, although Rabois planned to stay based in Miami.
Brad Gerstner , CEO of Altimeter Capital, had thoughts on how the US data center buildout would be affected by the elections.
In a guest appearance on the All-In podcast livestream Tuesday evening, Gerstner said fears that a "blue tsunami" could make it difficult to build new data centers are "overblown."
But he said that election results could slow down the development of the centers, and candidates like Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who won the Texas gubernatorial race Tuesday, could "issue a moratorium on new data centers." He said this could be "really challenging for the AI infratrade."
Gerstner also said that Republicans and the AI community have "struggled with the messaging" over AI as the affordability crisis has weighed on Americans' minds.
The investor is the architect of "Trump Accounts," the investment vehicle for children in the country that launched in July.
Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, hinted at what he believes a blue wave could mean for the AI buildout.
"I am now bullish space datacenters," Patel said in a post on X alongside a screenshot of results out of Texas that showed Hinojosa with an early lead over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.
Ahead of the midterms, some in tech expressed concern that Democratic wins would mean additional scrutiny on data centers, which have faced fierce opposition in communities across the US.
Dan Ives, a veteran Wall Street analyst and AI bull, said the midterms will put the brakes on the rapid construction of data centers.
In a post on X, he said the "Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House was a seismic shift that will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years."
Ives added that while some investors will prefer a slower pace, others will view it as added risk.
"We estimate 10% of data centers will not happen now," he said.
Richard Branson, the billionaire founder of the Virgin Group, wrote in a post on LinkedIn that the results of the midterm election are not just "a decisive repudiation of Trump" but also an encouraging sign "about the limits of money in politics."
Branson wrote, "As a successful entrepreneur, I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent on — mostly Republican — campaigns this election cycle, in an attempt to buy influence and control over public policy."
Branson added that voters looked past the "hateful and false messages" fueled by the billions spent on funding candidates, voting based on the issues that mattered to them.
"I hope this will prompt the next Congress to start a fresh conversation about the toxic impact of money in politics and the need for meaningful campaign finance reform," he wrote.

Anker announced a new indoor security camera that’s designed to watch your yard, driveway, or front porch through a window, instead of monitoring what’s inside your home. The new Anker Eufy Window Camera E10 takes a similar approach to the Wyze Window Cam that launched nearly a year ago . It installs right against a window using an including mounting sticker to reduce glare and reflections, but the camera doesn’t require any weatherproofing since it’s not enduring the elements outdoors.
The Eufy Window Camera E10 is available now for $79.99 through Anker’s online store and Amazon , making it more than twice as expensive as the $34.98 Wyze Window Cam . But the E10 comes with a few useful upgrades. Wyze’s camera is limited to 1080p, while the E10 has a much higher maximum resolution of 2.5K, capturing more detailed 15fps videos at 2,688 x 1,520.
The E10 also offers a slightly wider and taller field of view than Wyze’s camera at 105 degrees horizontal and 57 degrees vertical. But to accommodate a wider range of installations such as an upstairs window the angle of the E10’s camera can be manually adjusted up and down by 25 degrees using a wheel on the back to ensure the areas you want monitored are properly in frame.
Other features of the E10 include color night vision, AI-powered motion detection and alerts that can differentiate between humans, animals, and vehicles, and a microphone that’s limited to louder noises given the camera’s location. Footage can be recorded locally to a microSD card up to 256GB in size, or pushed to the cloud with an optional subscription. And while Anker claims installation can take less than a minute, you will have to deal with potentially routing and hiding a power cord since the E10 lacks a rechargeable battery.

articles.title_orig: CVS Health to split pharmacy chain from health insurance
articles.title_zh: CVS Health to split pharmacy chain from health insurance
articles.content_orig:
CVS Pharmacy will be separate from CVS Health, housing major insurer Aetna and benefits manager Caremark
CVS Health, the largest US healthcare conglomerate valued at $117bn, has announced its plans split off its pharmacy chain from its health insurance and benefits businesses, ending an era in which healthcare companies grew into vast conglomerates.
In their announcement on Wednesday, CVS Health said they will split off its 9,000 pharmacies, in-store clinics and mail order prescription business into a business named CVS Pharmacy.
A second company will keep the name CVS Health and house the major insurer Aetna and the giant pharmacy benefits manager Caremark, along with other businesses that provide home visits and primary care to older people.
The company has come under pressure from lawmakers and regulators over concerns that the healthcare giants, including CVS Health, UnitedHealth Group and Cigna, have become too dominant, leading to higher medical costs. The three companies control roughly 80% of the market. CVS Health in particular generated over $400bn in revenue last year.
A political pushback against healthcare gigantism has led Arkansas and Tennessee to pass laws aimed at preventing the companies from managing prescription benefits and running retail and mail-order pharmacies.
The Arkansas state representative Jeremiah Moore, a Republican who sponsored the state’s bill, told Politico last week : “The average American citizen is really tired of being pushed around and bullied, whether it be from the government or a monopolistic company.”
He added: “For far too long, they’ve taken advantage of these sick people, and it’s what I consider to be crony capitalism. They’re bending the rules to benefit their own bottom line.” Other states have proposed similar restrictions.
At the federal level, a bill introduced by the Missouri Republican senator Josh Hawley and Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren proposes an antitrust crackdown.
Hawley has described the legislation as “a major step toward restoring transparency and making healthcare more affordable for every American.”
David Joyner, CVS’s chief executive and chair, will run the healthcare solutions business. “Our history is defined by proactively evolving to stay ahead of what’s next in healthcare, and in today’s environment, that means delivering more affordability, greater access and a simpler experience,” said Joyner in a statement.
That marks a stark turnaround from CVS Health’s earlier opposition to legislative efforts to break up the healthcare giant, which a company spokesman said would “open the door to private equity stripping the entire U.S. healthcare system for parts”.
The announcement comes after a series of acquisitions that saw CVS Health expand into nearly every corner of the healthcare system. It began in 2018, when CVS and Aetna merged in a $70bn deal. Healthcare rivals, UnitedHealth and Cigna, also brought into the trend of harnessing an insurer, pharmacy benefits, and a mail-order business under one operation.
CVS Health, however, did not meet investors’ expectations for growth. In late 2024, its share price fell to $44, though it has since rebounded. The CVS Health breakup is planned for early 2028.

Election nights tend to rattle retirement savers, but Wall Street opened Wednesday more calmly. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ), the most widely held stand-in for the benchmark S&P 500, traded at $763.08 before the open on November 4. That was up 1.16% from its November 3 close of $754.35. Reuters reported that stocks rallied and the dollar dipped after what it called a Democratic midterm sweep. But one session tells a 401(k) holder very little. The more useful guide is how the index behaved in the weeks and months after past midterms. That record shows a steady winning run, along with a few sharp breaks.
SPY's monthly adjusted prices add dividends back in and go back to December 1999. That covers six full midterm cycles. The table compares SPY's October close just before each vote with its November close just after. The index rose in five of the six Novembers and finished flat in the sixth.
The 2002 and 2022 cycles stand out. Both followed severe bear markets, and in each case SPY rallied after the vote. SPY rose more than 5% in November in both years. The worst case was 2010, when the index closed in November exactly where it closed in October.

The smallest gain was 4.8% after the 2014 vote and the largest was 20.0% after 2002. In between came 13.9% after 2006, 11.2% after 2010, 14.6% after 2018, and 12.4% after 2022. That run fits a pattern we have tracked before: the year after a midterm has historically been one of the better periods of the four-year presidential cycle.
For anyone near retirement, there is a catch: even the good years came with painful setbacks. In 2018, SPY gained 1.9% in November, then fell 8.8% in December alone. It ended the year at an adjusted 222.8902, which was 7.1% below its level before the election. December also gave back most or all of November's gains in 2002 and 2022.
Even the 12-month periods that ended higher had real turbulence along the way. From November 2018 through October 2019, SPY returned 12.2%, yet at one point it sat 8.8% below its prior peak. From November 2022 through October 2023, SPY returned 4.2% and included an 8.3% drop. From November 2014 through October 2015, SPY returned just 2.4% and fell 8.5% between July and September 2015. In each of those three years, the post-midterm lift came with at least one drop of more than 8%.
This cycle starts from a higher level than most. SPY began Wednesday up 11.9% for the year and 265.9% over 10 years. Still, it went into the vote down 0.86% for the week and 0.85% for the month. A change in congressional control can reshape spending priorities, and the sectors most tied to Washington tend to adjust first, before broad index funds feel much of the shift.
Over the long run, Wall Street has tended to come out stronger after midterms. The Dow ETF's six-for-six record a year out backs that up. One of Wall Street's biggest AI bulls says the sweeping Democratic victory in the midterm elections will slow the pace of the AI data center build-out in the US over the next two years. AI-related stocks dropped on Wednesday, including Elon Musk-led SpaceX ( SPCX ) and EV maker Tesla ( TSLA ), which fell 4% before trimming losses as the rest of the market surged.
Shares of cloud provider CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and data center-related companies IREN ( IREN ) and Vertiv ( VRT ) also traded lower on Wednesday after Democrats won a majority in the House and Senate on Tuesday night and flipped governorships across key states.
"There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control, especially over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," Yorkville's partner and managing director, Dan Ives, wrote on Wednesday.
Those hurdles, Ives said, will slow the pace of 800 to 1,000 planned AI data centers across the US. The analyst pointed out that the biggest worry for tech investors and the AI trade is the state of Texas, where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from.
Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas Governor race over incumbent Greg Abbott in a surprise result. While Abbott currently has a moratorium on data centers in Texas, the prevailing view was that it would have ended were he reelected.
"Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout, which makes worries around the future of the data center buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors," Ives said.
This poses a problem for companies like Texas-based SpaceX, which has been building out its AI infrastructure and taking steps toward a potential merger with Tesla.
"SpaceX and Musk are clearly caught front and center in this spiderweb," said Ives.
"There will be a lot of negotiations and politics on this front especially in Texas which is the foundation of the AI buildout in the US … and Big Tech will need to embrace this new political landscape as of today," he added.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk wrote on X following the election results.
Data center concerns emerged as a key issue in the 2026 midterm elections, with candidates facing growing public opposition to proposed facility locations, the expansion of power infrastructure needed to support them, and concerns that rising electricity demand could drive up consumer costs.
One silver lining for investors may be that political headwinds will force a slowdown in AI capex. AI-related jitters have already weighed on the Tech sector ( XLK ) in recent weeks, with financing concerns hitting neocloud providers that rent out computing capacity, while semiconductor stocks have also retreated.
Long-term, however, Ives remains bullish on the AI trade, as "the Street still is way underestimating the future revenue growth and profitability" stemming from AI.
Fundstrat's Tom Lee is also largely optimistic despite the blue wave.
"President Trump exercises veto power vs any potential 'anti-AI' 'anti-data center' bills," Lee wrote in a note on Tuesday prior to the election results. He also noted that Democrats would likely embrace AI data centers because they bring money and jobs to a community.

articles.title_orig: McDonald’s plans new value bundles next year after US traffic falls in third quarter
articles.title_zh: McDonald’s plans new value bundles next year after US traffic falls in third quarter
articles.content_orig:
McDonald's on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results as traffic to its U.S. restaurants fell, leading to a slight decline in domestic same-store sales.
The fast-food giant reported a 0.2% decrease in sales at its U.S. restaurants that have been open at least 13 months. Even so, the segment performed better than the 0.5% decline that Wall Street anticipated, according to a survey of analysts by StreetAccount.
"In the U.S., we're encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value," McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a statement.
McDonald's same-store sales returned to growth in September after falling in July and August, CFO Ian Borden said on the company's earnings conference call. However, in response to an analyst question, he clarified that he did not say that U.S. same-store sales would be better in the fourth quarter.
Kempczinski said in August that the company's U.S. business was falling short on execution, particularly on the implementation of its value offerings. Like many restaurants, McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years.
To reverse same-store sales declines, McDonald's focused its marketing on its Extra Value Meals and restarted regional and national promotions on its mobile app, which are important to its most frequent diners.
As McDonald's tries to regain its footing in the U.S., the chain is also testing two new value menus, one with mix and match bundles and the other with set combinations of menu items, executives said on the earnings call. The offering that resonates the most with customers and franchisees will be rolled out across the U.S. in early 2027.
Shares of the company rose about 5% in morning trading.
Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
The company reported third-quarter net income of $2.49 billion, or $3.51 per share, up from $2.28 billion, or $3.18 per share, a year earlier.
Excluding restructuring charges and other items, McDonald's earned $3.57 per share.
Net revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion.
The company's same-store sales rose 1.5%, lifted by its international segments. That topped analysts' expectations of a 1.3% increase, according to StreetAccount.
McDonald's international developmental licensed markets business, which includes Japan and China, reported same-store sales growth of 4.2%. Wall Street was forecasting same-store sales to rise 2.1% for the division, based on StreetAccount estimates.
The company's international operated division, which includes top markets like Australia and Germany, saw same-store sales growth of 1.4%. Still, the business underperformed Wall Street's expectations. Analysts were projecting same-store sales would rise 2.1%, according to StreetAccount.
"In the majority of our large international markets, we're holding or gaining share," Borden said on the company's conference call. "It's a soft consumer environment, but we're doing well."
France was a weak spot, McDonald's said. Kempczinski said that franchisees in France recently voted on a strategy to turn the business around. In addition to a softer economy in the country, McDonald's has also seen short-term disruptions related to student protests.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Jumps 1,000 Points On Democratic Sweep of Congress — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Jumps 1,000 Points On Democratic Sweep of Congress — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks ripped higher on Wednesday as a decisive victory by Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections — and President Donald Trump's acceptance of the results — removed political uncertainty risk hanging over Wall Street.
Democrats won majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate, and scored victories in key gubernatorial races like Texas. The Democrats will now be a check on the policies of Trump, who's enacted business-friendly tax cuts, while also pursuing tariffs and a war in Iran that's boosted inflation.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average traded 1,514 points, or 2.9%, higher. The 30-stock index moved back above 53,000 for the first time since Sept. 8. The S&P 500 gained 1.7%, while the Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.9%.
Stocks extended their gains after U.S. crude oil fell more than 8% as Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for the election losses the Republican party suffered Tuesday. Brent futures traded more than 8% lower.
"There's just going to be even more pressure to end the war," said Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at One Point BFG Wealth Partners. "The American people have obviously expressed their displeasure with inflation and the price of gasoline, amongst other things, and maybe this just pushes for an end to it. We'll have to see."
Trump told The New York Times he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results and told The Wall Street Journal that he and Republicans would work with Democrats.
The rebound "was in part due to the president's initial tone and reaction to the results," said Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets. "Still more uncertainty looms, but one thing is certain, there will be gridlock and historically this is good for the market."
Shares linked to the economy that could benefit from a more stable environment led the gains. Walmart added 3%, while Bank of America rose 2.5% as investors looked for stocks outside of technology.
Heading into the election investors worried a Democratic sweep could weigh on some areas of the market , especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence build-out. Investors feared a big Democratic win could mean more restrictions on data centers nationwide. The Texas governor win by Gina Hinojosa, who's pledged an immediate moratorium in the key data center hub, added to the fears Wednesday.
Shares of CoreWeave were lower Wednesday, along with Elon Musk's SpaceX , which is headquartered in Texas.
Another reason for the bullish sentiment Wednesday morning was that history shows the market does well under a divided government , where fewer policies and regulations are able to interfere with the business outlook.
Andrew Slimmon of Morgan Stanley Investment Management said the markets "like gridlock — they don't like a party with too much power."
McDonald's shares rising modestly after better-than-expected third quarter earnings. The rally is also a reflection that "less bad" is outweighing "less good" on the sales front.
Although U.S. same-store sales fell for the first time in 6 quarters, but the 0.2% decline was less than the 0.5% that Wall Street expected. Although traffic was down in July and August, trends improved in September, providing some optimism going forward.
It was a very different story abroad though. International restaurants saw positive sales growth, more than offsetting the domestic sales decline. Same-store sales for International Operated Markets rose 1.4%, driving the rather mundane 1.5% growth across the entire company. But despite that strength in overseas sales, the rise was a disappointment since it was less than the 2.1% projected by analysts.
Shares of the State Street Communication Services Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLC) were up nearly 4% on Wednesday, pacing for its best day since April 2025.
Top holdings of the XLC were higher across the board. Alphabet was up nearly 5%, as was the Walt Disney Company, and Meta Platforms was higher by almost 2%.
Magnificent Seven stocks rallied Wednesday morning, breaking away from the broader artificial intelligence trade that was in a downturn.
The two exceptions were Elon Musk's Tesla, which slid 2%, and Nvidia, which was lower by 1%.
The AI trade more broadly was selling off, as investors dumped shares of the companies most likely to get hurt by greater scrutiny from a left-leaning Congress. Semiconductors fell 1%, as shown by the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX). And, neocloud stocks dropped 6%, according to the Roundhill Neocloud ETF (NCLD).
Shares of Coreweave dropped more than 7%, while Nebius fell more than 4%.
The State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLP) hit a fresh all-time record on Wednesday morning.
The fund, which was last up more than 2%, was led higher by gains in Dollar Tree , Constellation Brands , Estee Lauder , Doller General and Conagra Brands , among others.
XLP is on pace to finish the year with solid gains, having risen about 17% in the period.
— Gina Francolla and Sean Conlon
U.S. equities jumped at the beginning of Wednesday trading.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rocketed higher by 1,022 points, or 2%, just after the opening bell, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite each added 1.3%.

Private-sector job growth held steady in October, with gains spread across sectors, as the labor market showed fresh signs of stabilization, ADP reported Wednesday.
The payrolls processing firm said companies added 86,000 jobs during the month, the same as the downwardly revised total for September and slightly ahead of the Dow Jones estimate for 75,000.
Nasdaq-100 futures are up 929.75 points off their overnight lows, based on the current price of 28,545.50. Futures contracts tied to the benchmark hit a low of 27,615.75,  their lowest since July 30.
Precious metals saw strong gains on Wednesday morning as the Democrats scored a clean sweep in the midterm elections, flipping both the House and Senate.
Spot gold was 2.93% higher at $4,043.45 an ounce by 5:05 a.m. ET, while spot silver jumped 4.44% to trade at $51.98 per ounce, as traders reacted to the U.S. midterm election results.
Front-month gold futures added 2.9% to trade at $4,054.60, while silver futures were up 4.64% at $52.09.
Other metals seeing notable gains on Wednesday morning included platinum , which jumped 2.47% to trade at $1,465.30, and palladium, which was 5.93% higher at $989.
Renewables and healthcare shares are among the biggest premarket movers, trading higher after Democrats took control of the House and Senate. Meanwhile, neocloud stocks, as well as prison operators and defense names, lag the broader market.

Healthcare stocks also rose. UnitedHealth gained 1.8%, Molina Healthcare added 6.3%, Centene climbed 5% and HCA Healthcare advanced 7.16%.
Neocloud stocks, in contrast, turned lower, with CoreWeave down 3.6% and Nebius off 1%. Shares of prison operators and defense names also fell.

articles.title_orig: Israel's president to begin consultations with parties after election deadlock
articles.title_zh: Israel's president to begin consultations with parties after election deadlock
articles.content_orig:
Israel's President Isaac Herzog has begun consultations with political parties on whom to task with forming a new coalition government, after he received the official results of a general election last week he said had no clear winner.
Herzog told party leaders that "not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled" if they want to avoid a new election.
Neither the bloc of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his rival Gadi Eisenkot secured a majority in parliament.
Earlier, electoral officials said there was no evidence of irregularities and that unsubstantiated claims by Netanyahu's camp of Arab-led parties "stealing" the election did not justify delaying the results' certification.
The Shin Bet security service is investigating allegations of foreign interference in the election, but the head of the Central Elections Committee stressed that they would not fundamentally change the outcome.
In the election on 27 October, Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.
Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That makes them potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.
The role of Israel's president is largely ceremonial, but after an election they have the role of inviting a Knesset member to form a government. That person will be given 28 days to do so, with a potential 14-day extension.
The president has wide discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition. They do not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.
On Wednesday morning, Herzog was presented with the official results by Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg at a ceremony in Jerusalem.
"In recent days, we have heard voices trying to cast doubt on the election results and to undermine their legitimacy. This is a real danger," Sohlberg said.
"One of the foundations of democracy is the ability to have a peaceful transfer of power. This stems from the understanding that the will of the electorate obligates us all."
Herzog announced that he would begin the consultation process on Wednesday evening.
"In order to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable and good government here for the people of Israel, I expect the factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled," he said.
The president also expressed confidence in the Shin Bet's ability to investigate the allegations of foreign interference in the election and appealed for patience.
But he warned that Arab Israelis - who make up about one fifth of the population and often refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel - "must not be smeared".
"I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently. There is no place for them toward any community in Israel," he said.
Earlier, Sohlberg told a meeting of the Central Elections Committee that the Shin Bet's intelligence appeared to point to a "widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states", some of which were hostile.
It believed further investigation was needed to "connect the dots and determine the scale of the phenomenon with a high degree of certainty", he said.
Last week, Israeli media reported that the committee had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's foreign ministry said it categorically denied the allegation.
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party and an ally of the prime minister, called on the Shin Bet to arrest all the leaders of Arab parties and interrogate them "until these suspicions are fully clarified".
Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen accused Ben-Gvir and the prime minister of attempting to "steal the election from the public".
On Tuesday, Eisenkot alleged that Netanyahu and his Likud party were "trying to carry out a veritable pogrom against democracy and the rule of law".
His comments came after Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara rejected a reported demand by Shin Bet chief David Zini - an appointee of the prime minister - to interrogate four Arab politicians, saying no evidence of wrongdoing had been presented.
Likud accused Baharav-Miara of trying to "obstruct the investigation and to cover up this serious case of manipulation of the electoral process by foreign actors".

articles.title_orig: Secret police files released in Hungary, 47 years after fall of communism
articles.title_zh: Secret police files released in Hungary, 47 years after fall of communism
articles.content_orig:
Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, in a controversial move the government says will help Hungarian society heal itself from the traumas of 45 years of communist rule.
Critics say the move comes too late, that the files themselves are incomplete, and that the move risks sowing division and causing unnecessary anguish to family members.
The date of the opening is symbolic - on 4 November 1956 Soviet tanks rolled through Budapest and other cities, to crush Hungary's short-lived revolution.
"I ask everyone to treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity,"  Prime Minister Péter Magyar told reporters at the state archives in Budapest.
"Many families will now face difficult information, often related to a deceased relative," he added. "It is impossible to process a trauma without discussion and asking questions."
Magyar defended the move, which was a central promise of his election campaign ahead of his landslide victory in April elections, as the fulfilment of a promise made by those who toppled the Communist party in 1989 in Hungary.
In the ensuing decades, conservative, Socialist-Liberal, and Fidesz-led governments  have all contemplated, but ultimately refused to open the files.
Since 1998, it has been possible to apply for your own file, and for historians to research those of others. But many names were blacked out, and many files withheld by the post-communist secret services for their own use.
Over the past 36 years, there were frequent leaks of data from the files, as successive governments tried to damage their opponents. Many files were also shredded, as the Communist party lost its grip in 1988-89.
From Wednesday, the names and personal data of around 60,000 people recruited by the communist-era secret services have become available on the nyitottaktak.hu website .
A typical entry records the real name of the informer, their codename, date of birth, address and mother's name, their motive for recruitment - whether voluntary or because they were blackmailed or coerced - and the name of their handling officer.
Another batch of files, known as the "B-dossiers" are currently being digitalised, and will be made available on 25 February.
These will offer much more detail about the recruitment process, and the high or low value of the information they provided.
Critics of the opening of the files emphasise this point - that people will be too quick to judge those they find in the files, and unwilling to understand the nuances.
Around 150-160,000 people are estimated to have been recruited as informers between December 1944 and February 1990 in Hungary.
Many were blackmailed, with threats including loss of work or study opportunities, loss of access to medicines, or the leaking of information about their sex lives or addictions. Such intimate details will be carefully edited out of the current disclosures too.
Krisztian Ungváry, a historian who has long campaigned for full public access to the files, says access to information on what is recorded by the state against the citizen is a citizens' right, and should not depend on the whims of those in power.
"In the overwhelming majority of surviving agent reports, it isn't even possible to identify the agent, let alone their motives," counters an opponent of today's move, Zsuzsanna Borvendég, a historian and MEP of the far-right Our Homeland party.
Publishing the names of informers without fully explaining the circumstances of their recruitment and their activities risks misleading the public, she told Hungarian media.

New York Times Co. (NYT) reported $768.54 million in revenue for the quarter ended September 2026, representing a year-over-year increase of 9.7%. EPS of $0.68 for the same period compares to $0.59 a year ago.
The reported revenue compares to the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $763.48 million, representing a surprise of +0.66%. The company delivered an EPS surprise of +4.62%, with the consensus EPS estimate being $0.65.
While investors closely watch year-over-year changes in headline numbers -- revenue and earnings -- and how they compare to Wall Street expectations to determine their next course of action, some key metrics always provide a better insight into a company's underlying performance.
As these metrics influence top- and bottom-line performance, comparing them to the year-ago numbers and what analysts estimated helps investors project a stock's price performance more accurately.
Here is how New York Times performed in the just reported quarter in terms of the metrics most widely monitored and projected by Wall Street analysts:
Total Digital-only subscriptions : 13,220 versus 13,023 estimated by two analysts on average.
Total subscriptions (Digital & Print) : 13,760 versus the two-analyst average estimate of 13,565.
Total digital-only ARPU : $9.93 versus $9.87 estimated by two analysts on average.
Print subscriptions : 540 versus the two-analyst average estimate of 543.
Revenues- Subscription- Digital-only subscription revenues : $421.25 million compared to the $418.37 million average estimate based on two analysts. The reported number represents a change of +14.6% year over year.

articles.title_zh: ‘Fortnite’ Clarifies The Odds Of Opening A Pirate Shop Token Chest
articles.content_orig:
Fortnite launched its treasure hunting season this Sunday, which includes a One Piece collaboration that was one of the most anticipated collaborations of all time. No one expected a new item to steal the show, overshadowing the One Piece skins players had been requesting for years. Fans have been obsessing over the Pirate Shop access token, a recently introduced item that makes the whole Item Shop free for a fortnight. Thankfully, they might be able to end their search earlier than expected, as Treasure Hours are scheduled to begin soon.
This mini-season is all about treasure hunting. To go with the theme, there's a chance that players will find treasure in each chest. The most sought-after treasure is the Pirate Shop token , which gives players the opportunity to claim everything in the Item Shop for 14 days. It can be activated once before Dec. 15, 2026, and then again before Dec. 15, 2027. There are various types of treasure, ranging from gizmos to rare skins. Of course, most players are after the token, which is worth hundreds of dollars in V-Bucks.
The Pirate Shop token has taken over the lives of a majority of the Fortnite community. Gamers are spending hours of their free time in Battle Royale matches, looting as many chests as they can in hopes of finding this token. The exact chances of finding the token are unknown. Dataminer Blortzen's calculations indicate it's likely to drop about 1 in 2,000 chests. However, community estimates point towards one token in every 700,000 chests — a scary discrepancy for treasure hunters. While rare, its reward is so unbelievable that thousands of players have flocked to Fortnite to try their luck. It's been dubbed " Fortnite 's response to GTA 6 ," a game that is sure to draw millions of players away from other titles.
This frenzy is why some have already found a way to profit from it. AFK tools are being sold to farm chests while players stand idle. Accounts with the Pirate Shop access token are available for sale on eBay for thousands of dollars . If a teammate is lucky enough to receive a treasure, everyone gets the same reward, so players are even buying carrying services , allowing them to camp out during a match while someone else opens chests for them. Using software or services to automate the game and trading or selling accounts goes against Epic Games' terms of service and can lead to permanent bans.
Treasure Hours start on Oct. 8, and they will be live every Sunday until the end of the season. While it has not been specified whether these events will increase treasure drop rates, it's entirely possible. Epic Games' official blog post on this season says Treasure Hours will provide "boosted drops."
Fortnite senior director, Chris Yu, has also confirmed Power Hours begin this Sunday . Treasure Hour times remain unknown, but effects are expected to be revealed once the limited-time event hours are announced. If treasure drop rates are in fact boosted, this will be the optimal time to grind it out with some squad mates and open as many chests as humanly possible.

articles.title_orig: HP names former GSK chief Emma Walmsley as CEO

articles.content_orig:
Brit Emma Walsley swaps big pharma for big printer: Prep for PCs, ink, and lots of DRAM-induced headaches
HP Inc has hired former GSK boss Emma Walmsley to plot its course through choppy PC and print waters.
Walmsley spent eight years as the boss at pharma biz GSK and further back in time held various marketing and general management positions at L'Oreal. She has no track record running a tech company, though she was on Microsoft’s board.
“Throughout the process, Emma stood out for the strength of her leadership experience across multiple industries, the clarity of her strategic thinking and her ability to translate customer insights into new growth,” said Chip Bergh, chair of HP's board.
In the first nine months of HP's fiscal 2026 , revenue had jumped 10 percent year-on-year to $44.5 billion. The print business shrank in that time and PCs generated the growth. However, amid a memory crunch with supplies dwindling, analysts are forecasting PC market contraction in terms of unit sales.
Global PC shipments slumped 20 percent in Q3 as DRAM shortages forced up prices and customers opted instead to sweat their assets rather than replace their fleet of computers. Things aren't expected to improve in the final three months of 2026.
One beacon of hope for all PC makers was AI, yet many customers aren't buying into the story for various reasons.
Walmsley previously said that during her time at the top of GSK she created a "totally different company, in platform, in momentum, in talent, in culture," she told the FT . "I think in time… it will be recognized." She also dealt with activist investor Elliot Management, which operates in the tech industry and called for her to reapply for the CEO role at GSK, claiming her lack of science background was an issue.
Walmsley said: " HP is an iconic company with a defining role in shaping the future of work on a global scale. I’m excited to join the team and, together, move forward with clarity and conviction. We will focus on harnessing the power of the AI era and putting HP’s creativity and innovation to work to unlock new sources of growth and deliver lasting value for our customers, shareholders, partners and people."
Employees will be crossing their fingers that their new boss doesn’t borrow from the playbook of her predecessor - who hotfooted it to PayPal in February - by running multiple redundancy rounds, and shareholders will hope their stock price show sustainable improvement. If not, Walmsley may have to manage more interest from activist investors at the latest corporation she is running. ®

articles.title_orig: Russian hacktivists say they were behind freezer hacks, but speculation remains
articles.title_zh: Russian hacktivists say they were behind freezer hacks, but speculation remains
articles.content_orig:
French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies.
"No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.
Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.
Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.
Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.
But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.
While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.
Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.
Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.
In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers.
By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.
According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted.
"The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.
The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.
But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them.
"Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.
Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.
It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.
Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe.
"We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens.
"Even pots in Ukraine were left alone."
A third company - French cyber-defence firm Sekoia - also noticed scanning activity prior to the second wave of cyber-attacks, but said it could have been automatic scanning without malicious intent.
In a report to its customers, it said evidence suggested the nature of the attack aligned with activity of Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, which is being accused of carrying out so-called "hybrid warfare" cyber-attacks across Europe.
But Sekoia's research also points to Iranian regime hackers or hacktivists too.
"Iranian-aligned actors have an established record of targeting internet-exposed industrial control systems and previous incidents involved the same equipment in Israel and the US - both adversaries of Iran," the report said.
According to Sekoia, about 40 Israeli supermarkets running Danfoss controllers were compromised back in 2022.
Meanwhile in late August, freezers in at least six US military bases were forced into defrost mode, as in France. The controller models remain unconfirmed and investigations are ongoing.
"To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups," a Sekoia spokesperson told the BBC.
"Furthermore, as NoName057 is not known to effectively conduct operations beyond DDoS attacks and has a history of making false attributions, we remain sceptical of their alleged claim of responsibility."
Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks work by flooding a website or online service with internet traffic in an attempt to throw it offline, or otherwise make it inaccessible.
Authorities in several countries are actively investigating the hacks and warning supermarkets about potential future attacks.
But no formal attribution has been made.
None of the three cyber firms which have been gathering honey pot data are ruling out that it could be a teenager.
But with the degree of planning necessary the experts all agree it would have to be a well co-ordinated group - and if so, they would expect online bragging to surface soon.
Sekoia also said the possibility remains that all three waves could have been carried out by different and distinct groups or copycats.

Nintendo ROM supplier Macronix is leaving the business as demand for its data center memory booms.﻿
Nintendo is about to lose a major memory supplier for its Switch cartridges. The supplier, Macronix, announced during a recent quarterly earnings call that it would be gradually phasing out ROM production and is instead focusing on NOR flash memory for data centers, Taipei Times reports.
Macronix’s ROM revenue fell 39 percent compared with last year in Q3 2026, but its revenue from NOR memory rose 158 percent, and its revenue from NAND memory surged 768 percent year over year. According to Taipei Times , Macronix chairman and CEO Miin Wu said during its Q3 2026 earnings call that “demand for NOR used in data centers is very robust. Customers are chasing us for more capacity, demanding that we deliver more NOR flash solutions for data centers.” The company also reportedly “expects chip price hikes to persist.”
Although Sony has announced a plan to stop production of physical game discs starting in January 2028 , Nintendo remains committed to physical games, saying recently that it has “no plans” to ditch them . Physical games also remain a bigger portion of Nintendo’s sales than other gaming companies; Nintendo said in August that physical titles accounted for 38.5 percent of its games sales, which is higher than companies like Capcom .
Macronix’s exit from the ROM business comes nearly a year after Micron shut down Crucial , its consumer RAM and SSD brand, to turn its attention to meeting AI data center demand.

The 10-year Treasury yield fell on Wednesday as investors weighed big wins from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections and oil prices pulled back.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield was down more than 5 basis points at 4.898%. The 30-year bond yield declined more than 3 basis points to 5.293%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield dropped more than 4 basis points to 4.573%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
Democrats obtained majorities in both the House and Senate . Democrats flipped Senate seats from Republicans in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Maine and Texas. They also won key gubernatorial races in Ohio and Texas.
The resounding victory by Democrats could rein in government spending from the Trump administration, as it makes it harder for the White House to push legislation through Congress.
Traders at JPMorgan said one of the issues Wall Street is focusing on after the midterms is "reduced deficit spending."
"This can be achieved by asserting power over the budget and likely wading through a government shutdown," they said.
JoAnne Bianco of BondBloxx said that a stronger Treasury market in response "makes sense," adding that "a more divided policy environment should make deficit growth more difficult and potentially improve the fiscal outlook."
"Looking ahead, attention will shift back to geopolitics and the ongoing health of the U.S. economy," the investment strategist said. "For now, there appears to be no immediate move toward escalating tensions with Iran, which should help keep energy prices and inflation pressures contained."
Oil prices dropped on Wednesday, with Vice President JD Vance blaming the Iran war for the Republican Party's election losses. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 8% to around $88 per barrel, while Brent crude futures declined 8% to roughly $94.

articles.title_orig: Man fighting for custody of badger he nursed back from starvation
articles.title_zh: Man fighting for custody of badger he nursed back from starvation
articles.content_orig:
An ecologist in the Scottish Borders is fighting to be allowed to keep a badger that he saved from starvation.
Graeme Wilson was called out to help the cub, called Harriet, in April after she was found in a cattle trough 100m (300ft) from her sett.
Wilson nursed the badger back to health but believes she was hand-reared prior to this, and it would be impossible to return her to the wild.
NatureScot - which turned down his application for an educational licence to keep the animal - said it was continuing talks to try to find a "pragmatic solution".
Wilson runs GW Ecology, a small independent rescue and rehabilitation service at his home in Denholm.
It carries out surveys to determine whether protected species are present on the sites of proposed property developments.
He also leads bat walks, workshops and holds educational events about wildlife and how to protect it.
Wilson describes himself as an "experienced and trained wildlife rehabber" who has cared for a variety of wildlife over the years.
He argues that an educational licence could allow him to support public understanding of badgers, wildlife rescue and caring for a protected species.
He said that after rescuing Harriet,  it quickly became evident to him that she could not go back to where he found her.
Wilson added: "It was almost second nature when she saw the bottle.
"I have cared for injured badgers before and never have I seen something like it.
"It was clear then she couldn't be released back into the wild."
He said NatureScot, the public body responsible for Scotland's natural heritage and wildlife, had told him she should be returned to the wild or sent to a zoo.
However, he believes that releasing Harriet into the wild would only result in her being hurt or killed.
He said: "Badgers are companion animals, they are a social animal and unfortunately for Harriet she has decided that humans are her social group.
"Can you imagine Harriet approaching someone on a dog walk or in the street?
"There is only one way that would end."
He said a zoo would also be unsuitable for Harriet, arguing she would become lonely and suffer unnecessary distress.
"Harriet's upbringing means she needs human interaction, not to be put behind glass and stared at," he said.
Wilson said he would keeping fighting to hold on to Harriet.
However, he admitted there may not be a lot he can do, despite having the support of several badger rescue groups in Scotland.
Police Scotland has been made aware of the situation.
NatureScot said talks were ongoing to try to find a way to resolve the issue.
"We are continuing discussions with Mr Wilson and other relevant organisations to try and find a pragmatic solution to this individual situation," said a spokesperson.
"The welfare of the badger is, of course, key while we consider the circumstances of the case."
Paul Reynolds, who chairs the British Wildlife Rehabilitation Council (BWRC), said it was important to realise that rescue and rehabilitation was a specialist area of animal welfare.
He stressed it needed appropriate facilities, species-specific husbandry, veterinary input and a clear understanding of the behavioural and ecological requirements of the animals being cared for.
"There is a significant difference between responsible wildlife rehabilitation and keeping wild animals in captivity for educational or personal purposes," he said.
"BWRC firmly opposes the use of wild animals as educational animals and the keeping of wildlife in permanent captivity."
He also said habituation to humans "should not automatically become justification for permanent captivity".
Scottish SPCA advice is that any badger cub discovered outside its sett before it is about 12 weeks old - or about the size of a domestic cat - is likely to need help.
It said any member of the public coming across a sick or injured badger should not attempt to hold or touch the animal until one of its rescue officers arrives.
"Badgers can become aggressive if they are in pain or feel threatened; they can give a nasty bite and their sharp claws could cause serious injury, if you try to catch it," it said.
"You should also contact us if you find a badger during daylight hours as they may be struggling."

Posted By Joelle Daniels | On 04th, Nov. 2026
Grand Theft Auto 6 potentially having strong pre-order performance shouldn’t come as a surprise to anyone, since the title is shaping up to be one of the biggest launches in video game history. According to new data by analytics firm Sensor Tower , Grand Theft Auto 6 has seemingly already generated $751 million in pre-orders alone.
The firm’s sales tracker indicates that this massive amount of revenue has been the result of around 7.71 million copies of the game having been sold ahead of its November 19th release. The tracker also offers some details about the split in sales across PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. Sony’s console has taken a massive lead, with 74 percent of the pre-orders coming from PlayStation users. Xbox Series X/S has garnered around 26 percent of the pre-orders.
While the PS5 has a major leg up over Xbox Series X/S in terms of Grand Theft Auto 6 pre-orders, Xbox’s chief strategy officer, Matthew Ball, had said back in September that the company has been “very happy” with the results so far . He also noted that pre-orders on Xbox were in line with the company’s current position in the console market.
“Tom, we are very happy with GTA VI pre-orders,” he said in response to The Verge’s Tom Warren discussing pre-order figures being skewed heavily towards the PS5. “The title is breaking records for Xbox; we expect even more records will be broken throughout the fall, and our internal analysis shows our share of pre-orders to be matching our share of the console market.”
Along with there simply being more PS5 users than Xbox Series X/S in the world, the fact that Sony had signed a marketing deal with Rockstar Games has also likely played a major role in giving PlayStation a leg up when it came to pre-orders. Even the Grand Theft Auto 6 Extended Look showcase from August had a prominent logo at the end revealing that the gameplay footage was recorded off a base PS5.
Rockstar recently announced that pre-loading for Grand Theft Auto 6 will begin on November 10th . Along with this, the company also confirmed that players will need 212 GB of storage space in order to download the game.
The studio has also announced that more details about Grand Theft Auto 6 will be revealed as we get closer to its release. While the nature of these details remains unknown, speculation indicates that we might see more gameplay, and perhaps even information about how it performs on the PS5 Pro.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is shaping up to be an incredibly ambitious game, with head of development Aaron Garbutt recently revealing that players can even “have your life in the game” thanks to the number of activities and gameplay systems it offers. “You can really make the game what you want it to be at the time, whether that’s more of a roleplay experience where you’re buying cigarettes and beer in the shop and going on the train for the day, or going to a club.”

articles.title_orig: AI Data Center Boom Set for Upheaval After US Election Rout
articles.title_zh: AI Data Center Boom Set for Upheaval After US Election Rout
articles.content_orig:
It was a bad night for data centers . In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown, who has aired ads for months calling his opponent “the face of data centers in Ohio,” cruised to victory to flip a Senate seat. Democrat Chris Pappas, who when seated will be the nation’s first openly gay male senator, mentioned his opposition to data centers in his victory speech and drew massive boos from his crowd in New Hampshire—even though the state has no large-scale data centers under construction.
Elsewhere, two separate Republicans named Derek and Derrick, whose Democratic opponents labeled them “Data Center Derek” and “DC Derrick,” suffered losses in House races in Ohio and Wisconsin.
As part of last night’s shocking blue tsunami , voters selected candidates with tough policies on data centers at all levels of government, in a clear rebuke to the industry’s buildout in states across the country. Almost a quarter of all voters told NBC News that data centers were “crucial” to their vote, while nearly two-thirds said it was either a major or minor factor.
“The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics,” Greg Casar, the Texas Democratic congressman, said in a statement .
“Data centers and AI as a technology are fundamentally linked in many voters' minds,” says Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist working on AI. “So you can address all of the different concerns with data centers with regards to their energy or their noise, or their pollution, and there would still be significant concerns about what these projects are enabling and the effect is having on opportunities, prices, jobs, society.”
Perhaps some of the biggest shocks for the industry came in the governor’s mansions. In stunning upsets, voters elected Democrats Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Gina Hinojosa in Texas, while putting Cindy Holscher on the cusp of a potential win in Kansas. All of these candidates campaigned not just for increased regulations on the industry, but for data center moratoriums. A pause on data centers in Texas and Georgia especially, two of the biggest hubs for development in the country, could have serious implications for the hundreds of projects planned for each of those states.
“I think we will see the end to favorable tax breaks, and it’s clear that people like Greg Abbott were harmed by their history of giving those financial incentives to AI companies and data center developers,” says McCoy. “I think we'll likely see the appointment of regulators in various administrative bureaucratic bodies that pose more scrutiny on these projects and an increase in the enforcement of environmental protection regulations.”
Simply being anti-data center wasn’t enough to boost some candidates—especially Republicans. In Wisconsin, Republican Tom Tiffany, who hit Democrat David Crowley early on in his campaign with ads dubbing him “Data Center David Crowley,” lost his race. (Crowley got more aggressive on the industry as the campaign went on, indicating he would support a pause two weeks before election day.) So did incumbent Mike Lawler in New York’s 17th congressional district, who aired ads slamming his opponent’s past statements that New York “needs” data centers, conceded his race even though the Associated Press has yet to call it.
Throughout the campaign, data centers proved to be a bipartisan topic of concern , and caused fractures within the parties themselves. Earlier this year, WIRED reported how many of Donald Trump’s MAGA loyalists disagreed with the president’s support for AI companies and data centers.
But it’s undeniable that anger about data centers helped elect Democrats. In the weeks leading up to the elections, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee ran ads that highlighted Republicans’ support for data centers or the backing they had received from AI companies.
“Voters aren’t stupid. The data center story is a corruption story. It's an affordability story. It's a Big Tech CEOs influence story,” says Sacha Haworth executive director of the Tech Oversight Project. “That's what voters understood when they cast their ballots and that's why Democrats routed Republicans so, so hard last night, because Republicans could not tell the same story.”
Many of the candidates who won on stricter data center regulations did so despite massive injections of cash from the AI and data center industries to their opponents. In South Carolina, Building the Future, a new industry super PAC, spent $1.5 million to support Darline Graham; she lost last night to Democrat Annie Andrews, who favors a moratorium. (Andrews registered the URL DataCenterDarline.com in late September to hit Graham on her industry connections.) Building the Future also injected more than $1.5 million into the Kansas gubernatorial race to support Republican Ty Masterson against Holscher. And Michigan Democrat Will Lawrence, who made regulations on AI and data centers a cornerstone of his campaign, has declared victory (though without an AP announcement) over Republican Tom Barrett in one of the most expensive races in the country. Barrett had gotten $340,000 from Elon Musk’s America PAC over the course of the race.
“Despite poll after poll making it clear that the conservative rural working-class base was concerned about data centers and the impact of AI, too many politicians in Washington chose big AI’s money over their own base,” Amy Kremer, chair of Humans First, an advocacy group pushing for democratic oversight of AI, said in a statement.
In data center ballot measures across nine states, voters rejected future construction plans, approved moratoriums, and called for greater consultation with and accountability to local communities. Ten states put forth more than 40 questions about data centers on local ballots, according to Ballotpedia, including 21 in Ohio alone. Questions ranged from outright moratoriums to rezoning questions to restrictions on development. Just one county appears to have allowed for more data center development on their ballot, according to Americans for Responsible Innovation president Brad Carson, who was tracking ballot developments throughout the night.
Tech companies appear to be smelling blood in the water. On the day of the midterms, The Hill reported that environmental groups and Big Tech companies were working together as part of a “Responsible Data Center Development Collaborative” to create a framework for data center development. McCoy calls this kind of collaboration the “right next step.”
Meanwhile, as the results rolled in, Musk posted on X , “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”
